title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
The inspo
I came across a sports analytics project shared online in 2025 by Lou DiMuro that I really liked. It uses NFL player tracking data from the start of the 2021 and 2022 seasons to estimate, for plays where the QB throws a completed short pass, the probability the play will be successful. A short pass here is one where the receiver is at most 2 yards past the line of scrimmage when the ball is released. It has an awesome GIF showing the players’ movement as a play progresses with a live updating estimate (obviously inspired my video above). Very cool.
What counts as a ‘successful’ play in their analysis depends on the down:

On 1st down, the play needs to gain ≥ 40% of the yards needed for a new set of downs
On 2nd down, it needs to gain ≥ 60%
On 3rd or 4th down, it needs to gain 100%

What’s interesting is that the model needs to account for the yards a receiver might gain after the catch, which aren’t known at the time of the pass. It’s judged on the outcome of the entire play (not just the pass). Only completed passes are included (no incompletions or interceptions), so it’s essentially asking “will the play gain enough yards assuming it’s caught?”
It uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate the probability of a successful play at the moment the ball is released. A strength of CNNs is that they can learn patterns from complex, high-dimensional inputs (e.g., position and velocity of all 22 players on the field). This comes at the cost of some interpretability. They can be very good at recognising situations that make a pass more or less likely to succeed, but understanding why the likelihood changes or how much different aspects of the play contribute to it is hard.
Whether interpretability like this matters depends on what we want from the model. If the main goal is pure prediction, giving a flexible model access to the full tracking data makes sense. But in applied sport environments, analysts also need to explain and discuss predictions with coaches or players who need to make decisions and actually do things in the game. Those conversations often turn to what might have happened if someone did something differently.
A coach wants to know:

If I ask a player to instead do it this way, what can I expect to change?

An athlete watching film might think:

If I do this, how might the defenders respond and how would that impact the play?

These are causal questions that can’t be answered from observational play data alone. What can be done though, is to represent the plays in football terms and examine how those representations relate to success. For example:

How does the space around a receiver at the time of the pass relate to the probability of a successful play?
How does the nearest defender’s closing speed relate to the chance of success?

Putting the questions in football terms like this gives coaches and players something concrete to challenge. They might disagree with how I’ve represented space or closing speed conceptually, or whether the relationships found make sense to them based on their domain knowledge. That discussion might uncover something worth testing with a research design that can estimate a causal effect.
My aim here is to turn the data used to train the CNN into a small set of domain-informed “football features” (e.g., space around a receiver, blocker positioning, etc) and use Bayesian logistic regression to model the probability of success. The features make my choices about how to represent the play explicit, the regression model makes the relationships easier to inspect, and the Bayesian approach lets me quantify and carry the uncertainty in those relationships through to the predicted probability of success.
The question is whether the transparency gained by making those football concepts explicit costs much in predictive performance.

The raw tracking data comes from the NFL’s Next Gen Stats Big Data Bowl. The data is available on Kaggle, split across two competitions. Big Data Bowl 2023 contains data from weeks 1–8 of the 2021 season and Big Data Bowl 2025 has weeks 1–9 of the 2022 season.
With ~50 frames per play and the position of every player and ball recorded at each frame, the full tracking dataset is ~3.7M rows. You can download it with a free Kaggle account after joining each competition and accepting the rules.
I didn’t work directly from the raw Kaggle data. I used the preprocessed data from Lou’s project GitHub repo, which captures only the completed short pass plays and transforms the data into tensors suitable for modelling with a neural network. It includes 3,228 plays, and 59% of them were successful. Instead of re-publishing the full 100+ MB dataset, I’ve included one play in the reference repo’s format as an example to demonstrate how I transformed it.

example_play <- read_rds(file.path(data_url, "example_play_tensor.rds"))

flatten_play_data <- function(tensors) {
  defender_rows <- expand_grid(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3])
  ) |>
    mutate(
      # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y)
      defender_velocity_x = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 2L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_velocity_y = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 1L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        3L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )],
      defender_offset_lateral = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 4L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_velocity_relative_x = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        6L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )],
      defender_velocity_relative_y = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        5L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )]
    ) |>
    filter_out(defender_offset_downfield == 0, defender_offset_lateral == 0)

  blocker_rows <- expand_grid(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3]),
    offender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[4])
  ) |>
    semi_join(defender_rows, by = join_by(play_row, defender_slot)) |>
    mutate(
      offender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        7L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_offset_lateral = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        8L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_velocity_relative_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        10L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_velocity_relative_lateral = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        9L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )]
    ) |>
    filter_out(offender_offset_downfield == 0, offender_offset_lateral == 0)

  play_context <- tibble(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    down = tensors[, 11L, 1L, 1L] * 3,
    yards_to_go = tensors[, 12L, 1L, 1L] * 29.5 + 0.5
  ) |>
    mutate(
      down = pmin(4L, pmax(1L, round(down))),
      # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down.
      yards_needed = recode_values(down, 1 ~ 0.4, 2 ~ 0.6, default = 1) *
        yards_to_go
    )

  list(
    defenders = defender_rows,
    blockers = blocker_rows,
    context = play_context
  )
}

def read_rds(url):
    """An array saved from R as .rds, and its attributes."""
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".rds") as file:
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, file.name)
        parsed = rdata.parser.parse_file(file.name)
    converter = rdata.conversion.SimpleConverter()
    return converter.convert(parsed.object), converter.convert(parsed.object.attributes)


example_play, example_attributes = read_rds(f"{DATA_URL}/example_play_tensor.rds")


def flatten_play_data(tensors):
    n_plays, _, n_defenders, n_offence = tensors.shape

    def both_zero(prefix):
        return (pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_downfield") == 0) & (
            pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_lateral") == 0
        )

    play_row, defender_slot = np.meshgrid(
        np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), indexing="ij"
    )

    def defender(channel):
        return tensors[:, channel, :, 0].ravel()

    defender_rows = pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "play_row": play_row.ravel(),
            "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(),
            # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y)
            "defender_velocity_x": defender(1),
            "defender_velocity_y": defender(0),
            "defender_offset_downfield": defender(2),
            "defender_offset_lateral": defender(3),
            "defender_velocity_relative_x": defender(5),
            "defender_velocity_relative_y": defender(4),
        }
    ).filter(~both_zero("defender"))

    play_row, defender_slot, offender_slot = np.meshgrid(
        np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), np.arange(n_offence), indexing="ij"
    )

    def offender(channel):
        return tensors[:, channel, :, :].ravel()

    blocker_rows = (
        pl.DataFrame(
            {
                "play_row": play_row.ravel(),
                "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(),
                "offender_slot": offender_slot.ravel(),
                "offender_offset_downfield": offender(6),
                "offender_offset_lateral": offender(7),
                "offender_velocity_relative_downfield": offender(9),
                "offender_velocity_relative_lateral": offender(8),
            }
        )
        .join(
            defender_rows.select("play_row", "defender_slot"),
            on=["play_row", "defender_slot"],
            how="semi",
        )
        .filter(~both_zero("offender"))
    )

    play_context = (
        pl.DataFrame(
            {
                "play_row": np.arange(n_plays),
                "down": tensors[:, 10, 0, 0] * 3,
                "yards_to_go": tensors[:, 11, 0, 0] * 29.5 + 0.5,
            }
        )
        .with_columns(down=pl.col("down").round().clip(1, 4).cast(pl.Int64))
        .with_columns(
            # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down
            yards_needed=pl.col("down").replace_strict({1: 0.4, 2: 0.6}, default=1.0)
            * pl.col("yards_to_go")
        )
    )

    return {
        "defenders": defender_rows,
        "blockers": blocker_rows,
        "context": play_context,
    }

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
The football features
With the tracking data in a simple tabular format, I can start creating features that describe the play in football terms. Instead of feeding the model every player’s position and velocity directly, I define things that I think might matter (e.g., how far the nearest defender is from the receiver and how quickly they’re closing that space).
The data says where the receiver and defenders are, but I’m deciding which football concepts within those measurements might inform the outcome. Someone with a different view of the game might choose differently. That’s a limitation, but it also puts the assumptions out in the open.
The simplest example is yards needed. The CNN was given the down and distance and had to learn the success rule from the data. I already know the rule, so I just calculated the yards each play needs and gave the model that instead.
The model I built uses nine features covering six concepts:






R code · calculate and show the features
# The features for every play in a set of tables from flatten_play_data(),
# one row per play
# receiver_depth comes separately from the season play data, not the tensors.
# The line of scrimmage is at x = 60 after preprocessing, so receiver_depth
# is the receiver's x position at release minus 60 (positive beyond the line).
calculate_features <- function(tables) {
  defenders <- tables$defenders |>
    mutate(
      distance = sqrt(defender_offset_downfield^2 + defender_offset_lateral^2),
      # How fast the gap to the receiver is shrinking (positive is closing):
      # the relative velocity along the line between them
      closing_speed = -(defender_offset_downfield *
        defender_velocity_relative_x +
        defender_offset_lateral * defender_velocity_relative_y) /
        (distance + 1e-6)
    )

  around_the_receiver <- defenders |>
    summarise(
      # The nearest defender in front of the receiver, or the farthest
      # defender if nobody is in front
      space_ahead = if (any(defender_offset_downfield > 0)) {
        min(distance[defender_offset_downfield > 0])
      } else {
        max(distance)
      },
      room_beyond_nearest = space_ahead - min(distance),
      min_def_y_distance_to_rec = min(abs(defender_offset_lateral)),
      nearest_def_cushion = defender_offset_downfield[which.min(distance)],
      def_y_spread = sd(defender_offset_lateral),
      mean_top3_closing_speed = mean(head(closing_speed[order(distance)], 3)),
      nearest_defender = defender_slot[which.min(distance)],
      .by = play_row
    )

  # The nearest defender's closest offensive player, and their relative speed
  blockers <- tables$blockers |>
    inner_join(
      around_the_receiver |> select(play_row, defender_slot = nearest_defender),
      by = join_by(play_row, defender_slot)
    ) |>
    mutate(
      distance = sqrt(offender_offset_downfield^2 + offender_offset_lateral^2),
      relative_speed = sqrt(
        offender_velocity_relative_downfield^2 +
          offender_velocity_relative_lateral^2
      )
    ) |>
    summarise(
      nearest_blocker_advantage = min(distance),
      nearest_blocker_relative_speed = relative_speed[which.min(distance)],
      .by = play_row
    )

  tables$context |>
    select(play_row, yards_needed) |>
    left_join(
      around_the_receiver |> select(-space_ahead, -nearest_defender),
      by = join_by(play_row)
    ) |>
    left_join(blockers, by = join_by(play_row))
}

# The features for every play in a set of tables from flatten_play_data(),
# one row per play
# receiver_depth comes separately from the season play data, not the tensors.
# The line of scrimmage is at x = 60 after preprocessing, so receiver_depth
# is the receiver's x position at release minus 60 (positive beyond the line).
def calculate_features(tables):
    distance = (
        pl.col("defender_offset_downfield") ** 2
        + pl.col("defender_offset_lateral") ** 2
    ).sqrt()
    defenders = (
        tables["defenders"]
        .with_columns(distance=distance)
        .with_columns(
            # How fast the gap to the receiver is shrinking (positive is closing):
            # the relative velocity along the line between them
            closing_speed=-(
                pl.col("defender_offset_downfield")
                * pl.col("defender_velocity_relative_x")
                + pl.col("defender_offset_lateral")
                * pl.col("defender_velocity_relative_y")
            )
            / (pl.col("distance") + 1e-6)
        )
    )

    nearest = pl.col("distance").arg_min()
    in_front = pl.col("defender_offset_downfield") > 0
    around_the_receiver = (
        defenders.group_by("play_row")
        .agg(
            # The nearest defender in front of the receiver, or the farthest
            # defender if nobody is in front
            space_ahead=pl.when(in_front.any())
            .then(pl.col("distance").filter(in_front).min())
            .otherwise(pl.col("distance").max()),
            closest=pl.col("distance").min(),
            min_def_y_distance_to_rec=pl.col("defender_offset_lateral").abs().min(),
            nearest_def_cushion=pl.col("defender_offset_downfield").get(nearest),
            def_y_spread=pl.col("defender_offset_lateral").std(),
            mean_top3_closing_speed=pl.col("closing_speed")
            .sort_by("distance", maintain_order=True)
            .head(3)
            .mean(),
            nearest_defender=pl.col("defender_slot").get(nearest),
        )
        .with_columns(room_beyond_nearest=pl.col("space_ahead") - pl.col("closest"))
    )

    # The nearest defender's closest offensive player, and their relative speed
    blocker_distance = (
        pl.col("offender_offset_downfield") ** 2
        + pl.col("offender_offset_lateral") ** 2
    ).sqrt()
    blockers = (
        tables["blockers"]
        .join(
            around_the_receiver.select(
                "play_row", defender_slot=pl.col("nearest_defender")
            ),
            on=["play_row", "defender_slot"],
        )
        .with_columns(
            distance=blocker_distance,
            relative_speed=(
                pl.col("offender_velocity_relative_downfield") ** 2
                + pl.col("offender_velocity_relative_lateral") ** 2
            ).sqrt(),
        )
        .group_by("play_row")
        .agg(
            nearest_blocker_advantage=pl.col("distance").min(),
            nearest_blocker_relative_speed=pl.col("relative_speed").get(nearest),
        )
    )

    return (
        tables["context"]
        .select("play_row", "yards_needed")
        .join(
            around_the_receiver.drop("space_ahead", "closest", "nearest_defender"),
            on="play_row",
            how="left",
        )
        .join(blockers, on="play_row", how="left")
    )

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
The model
Each play is either successful or it isn’t, so I’m modelling the probability of success with logistic regression. The model weights the features, adds their contributions to a baseline, and turns the total into a probability.
The model is written in the probabilistic programming languages Stan (run from R) and PyMC (Python).






Stan code · the whole model
// Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the
// features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural
// spline columns, built in R, so their effect can bend.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                    // plays the model learns from
  int<lower=1> K;                    // columns of the design matrix
  matrix[N, K] X;                    // standardised features and spline columns
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> y;  // 1 = successful play

  int<lower=0> N_new;                // plays or frames to score
  matrix[N_new, K] X_new;

  int<lower=0, upper=1> prior_only;  // 1 = ignore the outcomes
}

parameters {
  real alpha;                        // log-odds of success for an average play
  vector[K] beta;                    // change in log-odds per standard deviation
}

model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta ~ normal(0, 0.35);

  if (!prior_only) {
    y ~ bernoulli_logit_glm(X, alpha, beta);
  }
}

generated quantities {
  // Pointwise log-likelihood, for leave-one-out cross-validation
  vector[N] log_lik;
  // Outcomes the model would expect to see, for predictive checks
  array[N] int y_rep = bernoulli_logit_rng(alpha + X * beta);
  // Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored
  vector[N_new] p_new = inv_logit(alpha + X_new * beta);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    log_lik[n] = bernoulli_logit_lpmf(y[n] | alpha + X[n] * beta);
  }
}






Python code · the whole model
# Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the
# features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural
# spline columns (see the next chunk), so their effect can bend.
def build_model(X, y, X_new=None):
    X_new = X.clear() if X_new is None else X_new
    coords = {"column": X.columns, "play": range(X.height), "new": range(X_new.height)}

    with pm.Model(coords=coords) as model:
        # Log-odds of success for an average play
        alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", 0, 1)
        # Change in log-odds per standard deviation
        beta = pm.Normal("beta", 0, 0.35, dims="column")

        pm.Bernoulli(
            "y",
            logit_p=alpha + pm.math.dot(X.to_numpy(), beta),
            observed=y,
            dims="play",
        )
        # Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored
        pm.Deterministic(
            "p_new",
            pm.math.invlogit(alpha + pm.math.dot(X_new.to_numpy(), beta)),
            dims="new",
        )

    return model





The model assumes seven of the nine features have a straight-line relationship with the log odds of success. For the other two (yards needed and cushion), I let the model fit a curve (using splines). This is because going from 1 to 3 yards needed for a successful play is a big deal for a short pass, but 12 to 14 (same +2 yd difference) barely changes the odds (already low). When the nearest defender is close, an extra yard of space can be the difference between a tackle and a catch with room to run. When the defender’s already far away or behind the receiver, another yard doesn’t change much.






R code · preparing the features for Stan
# Turn play-level features into the design matrix the Stan model is fitted on.
#
# Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots)
# is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the
# model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing.

SPLINE_TERMS <- c(yards_needed = 4L, nearest_def_cushion = 3L)

design_recipe <- function(train, features, spline_terms = SPLINE_TERMS) {
  linear <- setdiff(features, names(spline_terms))
  bases <- imap(
    spline_terms,
    \(df, feature) splines::ns(train[[feature]], df = df)
  )

  list(
    linear = linear,
    centre = map_dbl(train[linear], mean),
    scale = map_dbl(train[linear], sd),
    bases = bases,
    curve_centre = map(bases, colMeans),
    curve_scale = map(bases, \(basis) map_dbl(as_tibble(basis), sd))
  )
}

design_matrix <- function(plays, recipe) {
  linear <- plays[recipe$linear] |>
    as.matrix() |>
    scale(center = recipe$centre, scale = recipe$scale)

  curves <- imap(recipe$bases, \(basis, feature) {
    curve <- predict(basis, plays[[feature]]) |>
      scale(
        center = recipe$curve_centre[[feature]],
        scale = recipe$curve_scale[[feature]]
      )
    colnames(curve) <- str_c(feature, "_curve", seq_len(ncol(curve)))
    curve
  })

  reduce(curves, cbind, .init = linear)
}

stan_data <- function(train, recipe, new = NULL, prior_only = FALSE) {
  X <- design_matrix(train, recipe)
  X_new <- if (is.null(new)) {
    X[0, , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    design_matrix(new, recipe)
  }

  list(
    N = nrow(X),
    K = ncol(X),
    X = X,
    y = as.integer(train$success),
    N_new = nrow(X_new),
    X_new = X_new,
    prior_only = as.integer(prior_only)
  )
}

# Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays
recipe <- design_recipe(plays, final_features)






Python code · preparing the features for the model
# Turn play-level features into the design matrix the model is fitted on.
#
# Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots)
# is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the
# model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing.

SPLINE_TERMS = {"yards_needed": 4, "nearest_def_cushion": 3}


def natural_spline(x, df):
    """A natural cubic spline for x, Python's usual stand-in for R's
    splines::ns(x, df). Centring the columns leaves the baseline to alpha."""
    spline = f"cr(x, df={df}, constraints='center') - 1"
    return model_matrix(spline, pl.DataFrame({"x": x})).model_spec


def spline_basis(spline, x):
    """The spline's columns at x. Beyond the outer knots the curve carries on
    as a straight line."""
    return np.asarray(spline.get_model_matrix(pl.DataFrame({"x": x})))


def design_recipe(train, features, spline_terms=SPLINE_TERMS):
    linear = [feature for feature in features if feature not in spline_terms]
    splines = {
        feature: natural_spline(train[feature], df)
        for feature, df in spline_terms.items()
    }
    curves = {
        feature: spline_basis(spline, train[feature])
        for feature, spline in splines.items()
    }

    return {
        "linear": linear,
        "centre": {feature: train[feature].mean() for feature in linear},
        "scale": {feature: train[feature].std() for feature in linear},
        "splines": splines,
        "curve_centre": {
            feature: curve.mean(axis=0) for feature, curve in curves.items()
        },
        "curve_scale": {
            feature: curve.std(axis=0, ddof=1) for feature, curve in curves.items()
        },
    }


def design_matrix(plays, recipe):
    linear = plays.select(
        (pl.col(feature) - recipe["centre"][feature]) / recipe["scale"][feature]
        for feature in recipe["linear"]
    )

    curves = []
    for feature, spline in recipe["splines"].items():
        curve = (
            spline_basis(spline, plays[feature]) - recipe["curve_centre"][feature]
        ) / (recipe["curve_scale"][feature])
        names = [f"{feature}_curve{i}" for i in range(1, curve.shape[1] + 1)]
        curves.append(pl.DataFrame(curve, schema=names, orient="row"))

    return pl.concat([linear, *curves], how="horizontal")


# Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays

NotePrior predictive check and simulation-based calibration (technical details)





Do the priors make sense? Bayesian models like this one need priors representing our beliefs about the distribution of plausible parameter values. Because thinking about parameters and understanding their impact on observed outcomes isn’t natural to most psychologically well-adjusted humans, it’s good practice to simulate outcome data using parameter values drawn from our prior distributions. This way we can see if those choices of priors generate outcome values within the realms of reality.
In this case, the priors allow a wide range of plausible success rates (about 20–80%) that comfortably includes the observed 59%.

Can the model recover known parameter values? The prior predictive check above looks at whether the priors are sensible, but doesn’t validate that the model can find true parameter values. If I simulate data using known parameters drawn from the priors and fit the model to the simulated data, do the model’s estimates line up with the true values? Does each true value land in the middle half of the model’s estimates about half the time, in the top tenth about a tenth of the time, etc? Simulation-based calibration checks this by fitting the model 200 times on different randomly simulated datasets. Because it’s fitting the model 200 times, this part is computationally expensive (i.e., slow: about 15–20 min on my M5 MacBook Air).
In the chart below, each panel is one parameter. All but one of the lines stay inside the shaded bands (the third yards-needed curve pokes outside). The shaded regions are the area the line should stay in 95% of the time if the fitting works, so with 15 parameters one just poking out isn’t a concern.

sbc_data <- stan_data(plays, recipe)

# every real play from those parameters
simulate_dataset <- function(data) {
  alpha <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)
  beta <- rnorm(data$K, 0, 0.35)
  log_odds <- alpha + drop(data$X %*% beta)

  list(
    variables = list(alpha = alpha, beta = beta),
    generated = modifyList(
      data,
      list(y = rbinom(data$N, 1, plogis(log_odds)))
    )
  )
}

rng = np.random.default_rng(20261007)
n_sims = 200
X_matrix = X.to_numpy()


# One simulated dataset: parameters drawn from the priors, then an outcome for
# every real play from those parameters
def simulate_dataset(rng):
    alpha = rng.normal(0, 1)
    beta = rng.normal(0, 0.35, X.width)
    log_odds = alpha + X_matrix @ beta
    return np.r_[alpha, beta], rng.binomial(1, expit(log_odds))


ranks, divergences, rhats = [], [], []
for _ in range(n_sims):
    truth, simulated_y = simulate_dataset(rng)
    # The same sampler settings as the real fit
    with build_model(X, simulated_y):
        sbc_fit = pm.sample(
            1000, tune=1000, chains=4, random_seed=rng, progressbar=False
        )

    posterior = sbc_fit.posterior
    draws = np.column_stack(
        [
            posterior["alpha"].values.ravel(),
            posterior["beta"].values.reshape(-1, X.width),
        ]
    )
    # Where each true value ranks among the draws, thinned to every 10th draw
    # so the ranks aren't distorted by autocorrelation
    ranks.append((draws[::10] < truth).mean(axis=0))
    divergences.append(int(sbc_fit.sample_stats["diverging"].sum()))
    convergence = az.summary(sbc_fit, var_names=["alpha", "beta"], kind="diagnostics")
    rhats.append(convergence["r_hat"].max())

pit = xr.Dataset(
    {"pit": (("chain", "draw", "parameter"), np.array(ranks)[None])},
    coords={"parameter": ["alpha", *X.columns]},
)

    f"{sum(divergences)} divergent transitions across {n_sims} simulated datasets; "
    f"largest R-hat {max(rhats):.3f}"
)

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
Did it cost predictive performance?
Did making the football concepts explicit and using a simpler, interpretable model cost much in predictive performance? No. 
It performed as well as the CNN, and a little better on every metric the CNN reports.
To make the comparison as fair as I could, I copied the reference eval by using the same 3,228 plays, the same five-fold cross-validation approach (stratified, seed 42), and the same definition of each metric.1 That’s only possible because Lou published the plays, how they were split, and exactly how the model’s performance was assessed 🙌 (many don’t do this). Every prediction here was made by a version of the model that never saw that play (the code that does this is in the appendix).






R code · comparing model performance
# Area under the precision-recall curve by the trapezoid rule, with an anchor
# at (recall 0, precision 1). This is sklearn's auc(recall, precision), the
# definition the reference CNN reports, and it gives a slightly different
# number from the step-wise "average precision".
pr_auc_trapz <- function(prob, y) {
  n_pos <- sum(y == 1L)
  if (n_pos == 0L || n_pos == length(y)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  # A threshold includes every play with the same predicted probability.
  thresholds <- tibble(prob, y) |>
    summarise(n = n(), successes = sum(y == 1L), .by = prob) |>
    arrange(desc(prob)) |>
    mutate(
      true_positives = cumsum(successes),
      predicted_positives = cumsum(n)
    )
  precision <- c(1, thresholds$true_positives / thresholds$predicted_positives)
  recall <- c(0, thresholds$true_positives / n_pos)
  sum(diff(recall) * (precision[-length(precision)] + precision[-1]) / 2)
}

# Area under the ROC curve from the rank-sum identity.
roc_auc_fast <- function(prob, y) {
  n_pos <- sum(y == 1L)
  n_neg <- sum(y == 0L)
  if (n_pos == 0L || n_neg == 0L) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  ranks <- rank(prob, ties.method = "average")
  (sum(ranks[y == 1L]) - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2) / (n_pos * n_neg)
}

# The four metrics the reference CNN reports, as a one-row tibble.
performance <- function(prob, y) {
  tibble(
    pr_auc = pr_auc_trapz(prob, y),
    roc_auc = roc_auc_fast(prob, y),
    accuracy = mean((prob >= 0.5) == (y == 1L)),
    brier = mean((prob - y)^2)
  )
}

# Predicted probabilities in equal-width bins against how often those plays
# succeeded. `lower` and `upper` are a 90% interval on the observed rate.
calibration_data <- function(prob_mean, y, n_bins = 10) {
  tibble(prob_mean = prob_mean, y = y) |>
    mutate(
      bin = cut(
        prob_mean,
        breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_bins + 1),
        include.lowest = TRUE,
        labels = FALSE
      )
    ) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      n_success = sum(y),
      mean_pred = mean(prob_mean),
      mean_obs = mean(y),
      lower = qbeta(0.05, n_success + 0.5, n - n_success + 0.5),
      upper = qbeta(0.95, n_success + 0.5, n - n_success + 0.5),
      .by = bin
    ) |>
    arrange(bin)
}

# `reference` holds the cross-validated predictions (the code is in the
# appendix)

model_performance <- performance(reference$p_mean, reference$success)

success_rate <- mean(reference$success)

Python code · comparing model performance
def pr_auc_trapz(prob, y):
    """Area under the precision-recall curve by the trapezoid rule.

    Anchored at (recall 0, precision 1). This is sklearn's auc(recall, precision),
    the definition the reference CNN reports, and it gives a slightly different
    number from the step-wise "average precision".
    """
    n_pos = (y == 1).sum()
    if n_pos in (0, len(y)):
        return np.nan
    # A threshold includes every play with the same predicted probability
    thresholds = (
        pl.DataFrame({"prob": prob, "y": y})
        .group_by("prob")
        .agg(n=pl.len(), successes=(pl.col("y") == 1).sum())
        .sort("prob", descending=True)
        .with_columns(
            true_positives=pl.col("successes").cum_sum(),
            predicted_positives=pl.col("n").cum_sum(),
        )
    )
    true_positives = thresholds["true_positives"].to_numpy()
    precision = np.r_[1, true_positives / thresholds["predicted_positives"].to_numpy()]
    recall = np.r_[0, true_positives / n_pos]
    return np.trapezoid(precision, recall)


def roc_auc_fast(prob, y):
    """Area under the ROC curve from the rank-sum identity."""
    n_pos = (y == 1).sum()
    n_neg = (y == 0).sum()
    if n_pos == 0 or n_neg == 0:
        return np.nan
    ranks = stats.rankdata(prob)
    return (ranks[y == 1].sum() - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2) / (n_pos * n_neg)


def performance(prob, y):
    """The four metrics the reference CNN reports."""
    return {
        "pr_auc": pr_auc_trapz(prob, y),
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_fast(prob, y),
        "accuracy": np.mean((prob >= 0.5) == (y == 1)),
        "brier": np.mean((prob - y) ** 2),
    }


def calibration_data(prob_mean, y, n_bins=10):
    """Predicted probabilities in equal-width bins against how often those plays
    succeeded. `lower` and `upper` are a 90% interval on the observed rate."""
    calibration = (
        pl.DataFrame({"prob_mean": prob_mean, "y": y})
        .with_columns(
            bin=pl.col("prob_mean").cut(np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)[1:-1].tolist())
        )
        .group_by("bin")
        .agg(
            n=pl.len(),
            n_success=pl.col("y").sum(),
            mean_pred=pl.col("prob_mean").mean(),
            mean_obs=pl.col("y").mean(),
        )
        .sort("mean_pred")
    )
    a = calibration["n_success"] + 0.5
    b = calibration["n"] - calibration["n_success"] + 0.5
    return calibration.with_columns(
        lower=pl.Series(stats.beta.ppf(0.05, a, b)),
        upper=pl.Series(stats.beta.ppf(0.95, a, b)),
    )


# `reference` holds the cross-validated predictions (the code is in the
# appendix)
reference_p = reference["p_mean"].to_numpy()
reference_y = reference["success"].to_numpy()

model_performance = performance(reference_p, reference_y)

success_rate = reference_y.mean()

comparison = pl.DataFrame(
    [
        # Conventional no-skill PR reference; constant mean predictions for the
        # accuracy and Brier baselines
        {

            "accuracy": np.mean((success_rate >= 0.5) == (reference_y == 1)),
            "brier": np.mean((success_rate - reference_y) ** 2),
        },
        # Published by the reference project, averaged over four training runs
        {
            "model": "Reference CNN",
            "pr_auc": 0.7929,
            "roc_auc": 0.7314,
            "accuracy": 0.6808,
            "brier": 0.2026,
        },
        {"model": "This model", **model_performance},
    ]
)

    GT(comparison)
    .fmt_number(columns=["pr_auc", "roc_auc", "accuracy", "brier"], decimals=3)

    )

NoteWhat the four scores mean






PR-AUC (area under the precision-recall curve): how well a model ranks successful plays above unsuccessful ones, weighted towards the plays it rates highest. 1 is perfect. The no-skill reference is the overall success rate (0.59).
ROC-AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve): the chance that a randomly picked successful play is rated higher than a randomly picked unsuccessful one. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect.
Accuracy: the share of plays called correctly, counting anything rated 50% or more as a call of success.
Brier score: the average squared gap between the predicted probability and what happened (1 for a successful play, 0 otherwise). It rewards probabilities that are confident and right. Lower is better, and always guessing the average scores 0.24.




The headline metric in the CNN post is PR-AUC. The logistic regression model scores 0.827 against the CNN’s 0.793. This doesn’t mean “regression beats neural networks” (because often it won’t), but on this problem I didn’t have to give up any predictive ability to get a model that is more transparent about what contributes to a given prediction.
This compares the two approaches as a whole. My model also includes receiver depth relative to the line of scrimmage, which wasn’t included in the CNN’s inputs. Some of the improvement is from that extra context.

Can you believe the probabilities?
If a model says 70% probability of success, plays like that should succeed about 70% of the time. This characteristic is called calibration. A coach reviewing plays rated 70% should expect roughly seven in ten of them to have worked. If plays rated 70% keep succeeding only about half the time across lots of plays, the model is poorly calibrated.

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
What the model says
Yards needed for a successful play is associated with the largest change in estimated success probability, followed by receiver depth.
Here I look at how each of the six football concepts (rather than the nine individual features) is associated with success. For each concept, I compare the tenth of plays with the least of it to the tenth with the most, holding everything else at average. For example, going from the plays needing the fewest yards to those needing the most lowers the estimated probability of success by about 72 percentage points. Concepts associated with a higher probability of success sit to the right of zero, and those associated with a lower one sit to the left.

First, things the features don’t contain (e.g., the coverage, how good the receiver is, whether the throwing lane is open, etc) impact both the space around a receiver and how the play ends. Part of the reason why plays with space around the receiver succeed is what tends to come with the space, like a good receiver or a beaten coverage. That’s confounding and is why the model’s estimates can’t be interpreted as unbiased causal effects.
Second, every play here is one where the QB decided to throw and the pass was caught. Both depend partly on the space around the receiver and partly on those same unseen things. A tightly covered receiver might only get the ball when it’s a favourable matchup, and the throws into tight coverage that were broken up or intercepted aren’t in the data at all. Each of these makes tight coverage look less costly to the model than it really is. This is selection bias, and it also stops the model’s estimates from being read as causal effects.
The question a coach actually cares about (“what might happen if we change this?”) is a causal one and needs a different research design and stronger assumptions to answer. What this model and chart are good for is arguing with. For example, a coach might challenge the model by saying:

“Defensive width barely matters? That can’t be right.”

Maybe width matters through the coverage it signals, which the features can’t see? Maybe a standard deviation is the wrong way to measure it? That’s a conversation and opportunity to iterate that’s much harder to have with predictions from a neural network.

# Subset weights give the same average without evaluating every permutation.
# This explains the model's prediction, not the effect of changing a real play.
what_moved <- function(earlier, later) {
  idea_names <- unique(ideas$idea)
  n_ideas <- length(idea_names)
  subsets <- expand_grid(
    !!!set_names(
      rep(list(c(FALSE, TRUE)), n_ideas),
      idea_names
    )
  )

  probabilities <- map(seq_len(nrow(subsets)), \(row) {
    changed_ideas <- idea_names[as.logical(subsets[row, ])]
    changed_features <- ideas$feature[ideas$idea %in% changed_ideas]
    hybrid <- earlier |>
      mutate(across(all_of(changed_features), \(value) later[[cur_column()]]))
    predict_success(hybrid)
  })

    without <- which(!subsets[[this_idea]])
    contributions <- map(without, \(row) {
      with_idea <- subsets[row, ]
      with_idea[[this_idea]] <- TRUE
      matching_row <- which(map_lgl(seq_len(nrow(subsets)), \(candidate) {
        identical(subsets[candidate, ], with_idea)
      }))
      n_before <- sum(as.logical(subsets[row, ]))
      weight <- 1 / (n_ideas * choose(n_ideas - 1, n_before))
      (probabilities[[matching_row]] - probabilities[[row]]) * weight * 100
    })
    reduce(contributions, `+`)
  })

  tibble(idea = idea_names, change = list_c(changes))
}

def what_moved(earlier, later):
    """Exact grouped Shapley values: each concept's contribution averaged over
    all possible orders of changing the concepts from the earlier to the later
    frame. Subset weights give the same average without evaluating every
    permutation. This explains the model's prediction, not the effect of
    changing a real play. One value per draw, in percentage points."""
    idea_names = ideas["idea"].unique(maintain_order=True).to_list()
    n_ideas = len(idea_names)
    subsets = list(itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n_ideas))

    probabilities = {}
    for subset in subsets:
        changed = [idea for idea, is_changed in zip(idea_names, subset) if is_changed]
        changed_features = ideas.filter(pl.col("idea").is_in(changed))[
            "feature"
        ].to_list()
        hybrid = earlier.with_columns(later.select(changed_features).get_columns())
        probabilities[subset] = predict_success(hybrid)[:, 0]

    changes = {}
    for i, idea in enumerate(idea_names):
        change = 0
        for subset in subsets:
            if subset[i]:
                continue
            with_idea = subset[:i] + (True,) + subset[i + 1 :]
            weight = 1 / (n_ideas * math.comb(n_ideas - 1, sum(subset)))
            change = (
                change
                + (probabilities[with_idea] - probabilities[subset]) * weight * 100
            )
        changes[idea] = change

    return changes


def total_change(earlier, later):
    """The whole change in the probability of success, in percentage points."""
    return (predict_success(later) - predict_success(earlier)).mean() * 100

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
The limits
Every play the model learned from is a moment a QB chose to throw. The earlier frames in the videos are moments the QB chose not to, probably for reasons the features can’t see (the dashed box in the DAG above). So the number could be a bit off before the throw, and its interval doesn’t widen to warn you. Bridgewater might have held on to the ball through the peak above 80% because of something the model can’t see.
To summarise the limitations of my model (and of any model of this data, short of assumptions I don’t think hold):

It isn’t causal. It describes what tends to go with success (these are not instructions). It can’t tell you what would happen if a player did something different.
It only knows about completed passes. It never saw a pass that was dropped, missed its target, intercepted, blocked, etc. So its number assumes the catch is made and risky throws look better than they are.
It knows nothing about the actual throw. The features describe the space around the receiver, not the path the ball has to travel. A moment it rates highly might have a defensive lineman standing in the throwing lane with hands up.
Before the throw, it’s answering a different question. It learned from moments quarterbacks chose to throw, not moments they held on. See above.
It’s 3,228 completed short passes from the first half of two seasons.

title: Sometimes interpretability doesn’t cost predictive power
text:
The wrap
I wanted to see whether compressing the information from complex, high-dimensional tracking inputs into features representing football concepts would cost much in predictive performance. In this case it didn’t.
That doesn’t mean neural networks are the wrong tool. If nobody knows how to describe what matters, letting a flexible model find patterns in the raw data is a good approach, and it’s probably a sensible place to start with tracking data. What I found is that this outcome could be described well by nine features covering six football concepts. Once that’s true, the simple model is the easier one to inspect, question, and trust.
It also shows that football knowledge can go into a model, not just come out of it. Yards needed, the feature most strongly associated with success, is just the success rule applied to down and distance. The CNN had to learn that rule; I could just tell the model.
It could be applied practically in film review with players. Why does the model like one situation more than another? Does that match what they see? If not, what has it missed? It’d also be interesting to see which players consistently succeed more or less often than the model expects (implications on player evaluation and scouting). For real use though, I’d want a version trained on every throw (incompletions and interceptions included), not just the completed ones, and ideally one that also models when quarterbacks choose to throw.






NoteReproduce this




The analysis. Everything in this post runs from the files in data-public/, next to the post’s source on GitHub. You’ll need R with the packages loaded at the top of the post (dplyr ≥ 1.2.0; SBC installs from GitHub), my mitchhenderson package for the chart captions (remotes::install_github("mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson-R-package")), CmdStan and the Poppins font. The videos aren’t included because they contain broadcast footage.
The Python version uses the same files. You’ll need Polars, PyMC, ArviZ, formulaic, SciPy, matplotlib, great_tables and rdata (to read the example play’s .rds file). I ran it with PyMC 6.3, ArviZ 1.3 and Polars 2.0.
The features were built from the preprocessed plays in Lou’s repo.
The raw tracking data is on Kaggle (Big Data Bowl 2023 and 2025).

text:
Appendix

Cross-validation
Every prediction in the comparison was made by a model that never saw that play. The plays are split into five folds, and the model is fitted on four and predicts the fifth, once for each fold. The folds are made the same way as the reference project’s (stratified five-fold, seed 42), and centres, scales and spline knots are learned from the four training folds only.






R code · cross-validation
# Fit on every fold but one and predict the plays in the fold left out
predict_fold <- function(held_out) {
  train <- plays |> filter(fold != held_out)
  test <- plays |> filter(fold == held_out)

  fold_fit <- model$sample(
    data = stan_data(train, design_recipe(train, final_features), new = test),
    seed = 2534,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    iter_warmup = 1000,
    iter_sampling = 1000,
    refresh = 0
  )

  sampler <- fold_fit$diagnostic_summary(quiet = TRUE)
  convergence <- fold_fit$draws(c("alpha", "beta")) |>
    summarise_draws(rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail)
  if (
    sum(sampler$num_divergent) > 0 ||
      max(convergence$rhat) >= 1.01 ||
      min(convergence$ess_bulk, convergence$ess_tail) <= 400
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("Fold {held_out} failed its checks.")
  }

  probability <- as_draws_rvars(fold_fit$draws("p_new"))$p_new

  test |>
    mutate(
      game_id,
      play_id,
      success,
      p_mean = mean(probability)
    )
}

# A prediction for every play, each from the model that left its fold out
reference <- map(1:5, predict_fold) |>
  list_rbind()

def predict_fold(held_out):
    """Fit on every fold but one and predict the plays in the fold left out."""
    train = plays.filter(pl.col("fold") != held_out)
    test = plays.filter(pl.col("fold") == held_out)
    fold_recipe = design_recipe(train, final_features)

    with build_model(
        design_matrix(train, fold_recipe),
        train["success"].to_numpy(),
        design_matrix(test, fold_recipe),
    ):
        fold_fit = pm.sample(
            1000, tune=1000, chains=4, random_seed=2534, progressbar=False
        )

    convergence = az.summary(fold_fit, var_names=["alpha", "beta"], kind="diagnostics")
    if (
        fold_fit.sample_stats["diverging"].sum() > 0
        or convergence["r_hat"].max() >= 1.01
        or min(convergence["ess_bulk"].min(), convergence["ess_tail"].min()) <= 400
    ):
        raise RuntimeError(f"Fold {held_out} failed its checks.")

    return test.with_columns(
        p_mean=fold_fit.posterior["p_new"].mean(("chain", "draw")).values
    )

text:
Historical distribution of wins

I could then use this match level data to calculate the competition ladder at the end of the season for each year in the data set.       made_finals = if_else(regular_season_position <= 8, 1, 0),

def competition_table(df):
    home_stats = (
        df.group_by("season", "home")
        .agg(
            pl.col("home_win").sum().alias("home_wins"),
            pl.col("points_differential").sum().alias("home_for_and_against"),
        )
        .rename({"home": "team"})
    )

    away_stats = (
        df.group_by("season", "away")
        .agg(
            pl.col("away_win").sum().alias("away_wins"),
            (pl.col("points_differential").sum() * -1).alias("away_for_and_against"),
        )
        .rename({"away": "team"})
    )

    draw_stats = (
        df.group_by("season", "home")
        .agg(pl.col("draw").sum().alias("draw"))
        .rename({"home": "team"})
    )

    return (
        home_stats.join(away_stats, on=["season", "team"], how="left")
        .join(draw_stats, on=["season", "team"], how="left")
        .with_columns(
            (pl.col("home_wins") + pl.col("away_wins") + pl.col("draw") * 0.5).alias(
                "total_wins"
            ),
            (pl.col("home_for_and_against") + pl.col("away_for_and_against")).alias(
                "for_and_against"
            ),
        )
        .select("season", "team", "total_wins", "for_and_against")
        .sort(
            ["season", "total_wins", "for_and_against"],
            descending=[False, True, True],
            maintain_order=True,
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.int_range(1, pl.len() + 1)
            .over("season")
            .alias("regular_season_position")
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.when(pl.col("regular_season_position") <= 8)
            .then(1)
            .otherwise(0)
            .alias("made_finals")
        )
    )

def _stack_positions(values: list[float]) -> list[int]:
    seen: dict[float, int] = {}
    positions = []
    for v in values:
        idx = seen.get(v, 0)
        positions.append(idx)
        seen[v] = idx + 1
    return positions


def make_finals_dot_plot(
    df: pl.DataFrame,
    colours: tuple[str, str] = ("#b5b5b5", "#c0392b"),
    title: str | None = None,
    subtitle: str = "Each circle is one team's season. Teams with the same number of wins are stacked on top of each other.",
    caption: str | None = None,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (11, 7),
):
    """
    df must contain: season, team, total_wins, made_finals (0/1) — i.e. the
    output of competition_table().
    """
    df = df.sort("made_finals")  # made_finals == 0 drawn first (sits at the bottom)

    x = df["total_wins"].to_list()
    made_finals = df["made_finals"].to_list()

    stack_idx = _stack_positions(x)
    radius = 0.24
    spacing = 2 * radius + 0.08

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)

    for xi, made, s_idx in zip(x, made_finals, stack_idx):
        y = spacing / 2 + s_idx * spacing
        ax.add_patch(
            Circle(
                (xi, y),
                radius,
                facecolor=colours[1] if made == 1 else colours[0],
                edgecolor="black",
                linewidth=0.4,
                zorder=3,
            )
        )

    max_stack = max(stack_idx) + 1
    x_min, x_max = min(x), max(x)
    ax.set_xlim(x_min - 1, x_max + 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max_stack * spacing + spacing * 0.5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")

    # --- axes / theme ---
    ax.set_xticks(range(int(x_min), int(x_max) + 2))
    ax.set_xlabel("Matches won", labelpad=10)
    for side in ("left", "top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#333333")
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_ylabel("")

    if title is None:
        title = (
            f"NRL teams have needed as few as {x_min:g} and as many as "
            f"{x_max:g} wins to make the finals"
        )
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", loc="left", pad=30)

There are a few ways to approach calculating the probability of making the finals based on a given number of wins. Doing this requires a mindset shift from thinking only about the outcome of a single event (qualify for finals vs not) to considering the expected frequency of an outcome occurring over a large number of events involving uncertainty and randomness.

title: How many wins do NRL teams need to make the finals?
text:
Analytically derive the probability
If this is possible, god knows I don’t know how to do it. Given the complexity of the competition structure with all its dependencies and constraints, specifying the true mathematical probability would be an extremely high-dimensional optimisation problem. Even if it is possible, it would require a very sophisticated and computationally intensive solution.2

title: How many wins do NRL teams need to make the finals?
section: Simply calculate the proportion of teams that qualified for each number of wins the data set
text:
Simply calculate the proportion of teams that qualified for each number of wins the data set
This isn’t a good idea. With 17 teams and each of them playing 24 games in a season, the number of ways a season could play out to determine the final competition ladder is astronomically large. We only have 10 seasons of data; a tiny fraction of all the possible combinations of win-loss records and finals standings to use in our calculation. The true probability of making the finals can’t be estimated with acceptable accuracy based on such a small sample of data. To demonstrate, the data we have shows no teams with 11 wins qualifying for the finals (from 8 times this has occurred). Does that mean the probability of qualifying is 0%? No. This is just noise (i.e., random variability) that we happen to have observed in our sample. Evidence of this is a team that only won 10 games qualified for the finals in a different season.

title: How many wins do NRL teams need to make the finals?
section: Fitting a linear model to the data
text:
Fitting a linear model to the data
This also isn’t a good idea. On the surface, a logistic regression model sounds okay as we’re trying to estimate the probability of a binary outcome (making the finals or not), but the assumptions baked into these models aren’t a great fit for this problem. Statistical models need to make assumptions so the complexity of the world can be simplified into something quantifiable and useful. In the case of generalised linear models like logistic regression, one of those assumptions is a linear relationship between the predictors and the transformed outcome. This is often useful because as it allows a smooth curve to be fit through the data, but it breaks down here without awareness of the fundamental competition constraints (e.g., for one team to win, the other has to lose). This means that they can (and do in this case) predict impossible scenarios like making the finals with a win-loss record that is mathematically impossible for them to qualify.

title: How many wins do NRL teams need to make the finals?
text:
Monte Carlo simulation
These are a class of methods that basically use randomness to solve problems. They allow us to skip most of the hard maths and use computer simulations to get practically the same answers that could have very painfully been calculated analytically anyway. The idea is that we define a data generating process that mimics the way that data is generated in the real world, and then let the power of computers generate a huge amount of data. This lets us explore tens or hundreds of thousand (or more) possible season outcomes to give us a fuller picture of the probability of making the finals for each win-loss record. This is especially important for edge cases and unusual season results that are unlikely to have occurred in a small sample of historical data like ours. The beauty is that we can build in all the dependencies and constraints of the competition structure so we know the simulated data generated will adhere to it. It’ll capture the non-linear and threshold effects that exist as a result of the competition format. With enough simulated seasons, we can simply count the proportion of teams that qualify for a given number of wins to estimate the probability. The law of large numbers tells us this converges to the true probability.

Simulating a season draw
To begin defining the data generating process, we need a way to randomly generate a season draw. This was tricky. 17 teams need to play 24 matches against other teams, 12 home and 12 away, where you play 8 teams twice and the other 8 teams only once (and of course accounting for the dependencies of head-to-head matches so one team’s schedule can’t be considered in isolation). I found a way to do it using network graph theory.






Code
# Define vector of team names
teams <- unique(data$home)

# Create random graph with 17 nodes (teams)
# Connect each node to 12 other nodes for home games and another 12 for away games
# Convert to tibble and add team names
simulate_season_draw <- function() {
  graph <- sample_degseq(
    rep(12, length(teams)),
    rep(12, length(teams)),
    method = "fast.heur.simple"
  )

  edges <- as_edgelist(graph)

  tibble(
    home = teams[edges[, 1]],
    away = teams[edges[, 2]]
  )
}

# Convert to a DataFrame and add team names
def simulate_season_draw():
    graph = igraph.Graph.Degree_Sequence(
        [12] * len(teams),
        [12] * len(teams),
        method="fast_heur_simple",
    )

    edges = graph.get_edgelist()

    return pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "home": [teams[home] for home, away in edges],
            "away": [teams[away] for home, away in edges],
        }
    )

Accounting for team quality
Because this distribution is so unique, I’ll randomly sample directly from it to populate the match results in my simulated seasons (instead of sampling from a theoretical distribution). I don’t want to sample completely at random though, because the teams are not of equal quality. I want the better teams to have a higher probability of winning against the worse teams, weighted by how much better / worse they are. To do this, we need a measure of each team’s strength. There are many ways to approach this, but for simplicity I’ll just use the Sportsbet odds for winning the 2025 competition.
The bookmaker odds are converted to an implied probability of winning the competition. This will be my measure of relative team quality.

Accounting for home field advantage
Next I need to account for home field advantage. Home teams won ~55.8% of games in the data set (1,084/1,944). If two teams of equal quality play, I want to adjust the probability of winning for the home team from 50% (based only on relative team quality) to ~55.8% so it matches the proportion of home wins observed in the 10 seasons of data. For two equally matched teams, the win probability model simplifies to m / (m + 1), where m is the home advantage multiplier, so I can solve directly for the multiplier that returns ~55.8% home win probability against equally matched opponents.






Code
perc_home_win <- mean(data$points_differential > 0)

# We know that for equally matched teams:
# 1. Without home advantage, each team has 50% chance of winning
# 2. Historical data shows home teams actually win 55.8% of the time
# 3. We need a multiplier that turns 50-50 into 55.8-44.2 (assuming no draws)

# For equal team strengths (both 0.5), the win probability model
# (adjusted_home / (adjusted_home + away_strength)) simplifies to
# m / (m + 1), which can be solved directly for the multiplier
# that produces the observed home win rate
optimal_multiplier <- perc_home_win / (1 - perc_home_win)

# We know that for equally matched teams:
# 1. Without home advantage, each team has 50% chance of winning
# 2. Historical data shows home teams actually win 55.8% of the time
# 3. We need a multiplier that turns 50-50 into 55.8-44.2 (assuming no draws)

# For equal team strengths (both 0.5), the win probability model
# (adjusted_home / (adjusted_home + away_strength)) simplifies to
# m / (m + 1), which can be solved directly for the multiplier
# that produces the observed home win rate
optimal_multiplier=perc_home_win / (1 - perc_home_win)





This method carries some simplifying assumptions. In reality, some teams are pretty likely to benefit more from playing at home than others. That isn’t accounted for here (all teams will be given the same home advantage based on historical data). Also the multiplier used to apply the home team advantage was found by optimising for the win rate between two teams of equal quality. This was to best isolate the degree of home advantage without the influence of differences in team quality. The mathematically optimal multiplier will change with each difference in relative team quality (e.g., unequally matched teams).


Simulate the match results
Now I can finally define a function that simulates a match. It compares the implied probability of winning the competition after accounting for home field advantage to calculate the home team win probability for the game. A random number is drawn from a uniform distribution (0 to 1) and if this number is less than the home win probability, then the match is assigned as a home win. Once we know whether the home or away team wins, a random sample is drawn from either the positive (home wins) or negative (away wins) observed points differential distribution (i.e., empirical distribution).






Code
# Function to simulate a single match
simulate_match <- function(home_strength, away_strength, diff_vector) {
  home_advantage_multiplier <- optimal_multiplier

  # Apply home advantage to home team's strength
  adjusted_home_strength <- home_strength * home_advantage_multiplier

  # Calculate win probabilities based on Sportsbet's Grand Final win probabilities
  home_win_prob <- adjusted_home_strength /
    (adjusted_home_strength + away_strength)

  # Compare to uniform distribution to determine if it's a home win or away win
  is_home_win <- runif(1) < home_win_prob

  # Sample the differential
  if (is_home_win) {
    diff <- sample(diff_vector[diff_vector > 0], 1)
  } else {
    diff <- -sample(diff_vector[diff_vector > 0], 1)
  }

  return(diff)
}






Code
# Function to simulate a single match
def simulate_match(home_strength, away_strength, diff_vector):

    home_advantage_multiplier=optimal_multiplier

    # Apply home advantage to home team's strength
    adjusted_home_strength=home_strength * home_advantage_multiplier

    # Calculate win probabilities based on Sportsbet's Grand Final win probabilities
    home_win_prob=adjusted_home_strength / (adjusted_home_strength + away_strength)

    # Compare to uniform distribution to determine if it's a home win or away win
    is_home_win=np.random.uniform(size=1) < home_win_prob

    # Sample the differential
    positive_diffs = diff_vector.filter(diff_vector > 0)

    if is_home_win:
        diff=np.random.choice(positive_diffs)
    else:
        diff=-np.random.choice(positive_diffs)

    return diff

Notice how most of the values are negative (meaning the away team won).
This incorporates the away team being of higher quality (20% chance of winning the competition vs 5%) and the home team benefiting from the home field advantage. There are again some simplifications at play here. Firstly, draws/ties are not considered (or possible) with this data generating process. I think this is fine as only 0.25% of matches in the data set ended in draws (5 from 1,944). Secondly, within home wins or away wins, the sampling of the points differential is completely random. This means that if a home team has been assigned the win, the amount they win by doesn’t consider the difference in team quality or home field advantage. The winning amount is completely random within the winning point differentials in the data set. Team strength values and home field advantage only influence who wins. I also don’t think this threatens the validity of the results (only for and against values will be affected), but worth mentioning as it is a simplifying assumption that I doubt is true in reality.

If you’ve taken statistics classes at uni you’ll probably have come across a similar idea to this with coin flips or finding pi. Basically, the average of a small group of numbers varies a lot, but stabilises as the sample gets larger. This is why we generally don’t want to infer things about a population based only on a small sample, we might just be interpreting the early variation before the stable number (that converges on the true value) is found. The finals probability for each win count in the animation doesn’t really become stable until around 250 seasons. Making inferences after only 10 seasons (like using the data we had) would have given us an unreliable estimate.
In summary, Monte Carlo simulations offer a practical way to estimate things (like finals probabilities in the NRL) when the calculations become mathematically complex or the sample of available data is relatively small.

text:
Step 1
Create a folder that will contain all your folders of Openfield 10Hz exports. Name this anything you like.
This folder will need to be in your working directory when you run the code below. If you aren’t familiar with a working directory, it is just a file path on your computer that sets the default location of any files you read into R, or save out of R. Think of it like a “home” folder and you refer to all files relative to this (you can check what it’s currently set to by running getwd(). I recommend using RStudio Projects to make this process much smoother.
In my code below I’ve assigned the variable folder_name to be “combine” (the name of my folder that I will save the export files). You will need to change the folder_name variable to the folder that will contain your export files.

title: Tidying Catapult 10Hz export data
text:
Step 2
Export the files you’d like to combine from Openfield without changing their filename and save them in the folder discussed in Step 1.
Some examples could be “Round 1” if you’re combining all your athletes exports from a round 1 match.

title: Tidying Catapult 10Hz export data
text:
Step 3
Make sure you have R and RStudio downloaded and installed on your machine (both free!).
Open RStudio, copy and paste the code below into a script (you can create a new R script by clicking the symbol directly under ‘File’ on the top-left of the window, and selecting ‘R Script’).
Save the file as a .R file with an appropriate name (e.g. “tidy_catapult_data.R”).

# Script to combine and tidy multiple Catapult Openfield 10Hz export .csv files by Mitch Henderson

library(tidyverse)
library(zoo)

# This must exactly match the folder name containing the .csv files and be in your working directory

folder_name <- "combine"

# This function will read in multiple .csv files, create a column with the file name, and parse it into it's relevant components.

read_plus <- function(flnm) {
  read_csv(flnm, skip = 8) |>
    mutate(Filename = flnm,
           without_folder = str_split(Filename, "/")[[1]][2],
           Activity = str_split(without_folder, " Export")[[1]][1],
           Player_interim = str_split(without_folder, " for ")[[1]][2],
           Player = paste0(
             str_split(Player_interim, " ")[[1]][1],
             " ",
             str_split(Player_interim, " ")[[1]][2]
             )
           ) |>
  select(-Filename,
         -Player_interim,
         -without_folder)
}

# Import all files contained within the folder specified by `folder_name` above

combine_and_tidy <-
  list.files(path = paste0(folder_name, "/"),
             pattern = "*.csv", 
             full.names = T) |>
  map_df(~read_plus(.))

# Output csv into working directory

write.csv(combine_and_tidy, file = paste0(folder_name, "_tidy.csv"), row.names = F)

title: Making better visualisations using ggplot2 in R
text:
Written in 2020. Kept for reference; it doesn't reflect how I work now.


“The ability to take data—to be able to understand it, to process it, to extract value from it, to visualize it, to communicate it—that’s going to be a hugely important skill in the next decades, … because now we really do have essentially free and ubiquitous data. So the complimentary scarce factor is the ability to understand that data and extract value from it.”

— Hal Varian, The McKinsey Quarterly, Jan 2009


Great results and important messages from sports scientists and S&C coaches are too often lost at the final and most important hurdle of the scientific process: communication.
A clear, considered, and engaging visualisation helps by presenting the data in a way that’s digestible to people, not just machines.
On the 13th April 2020, I tweeted a thread of visualisations that I’d made recreating the work of Tom Worville of The Athletic.


Inspired by the work of @Worville showing @LFC’s age profile over the past few seasons, I tried to recreate his charts for some other competition-winning 🏆 teams over the last few years using #ggplot in #rstats. A thread.1/6 pic.twitter.com/F9m4oVbLG0

The full code will be posted at the end, as throughout the post I’ll be going through parts of it bit by bit.
